content: Gas laws describe the relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and quantity of a gas. Boyle's Law states that pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature (PâVâ = PâVâ). When pumping a bicycle tire, the decreasing volume in the pump increases pressure, forcing air into the tire. Charles's Law establishes that volume and temperature are directly proportional at constant pressure (Vâ/Tâ = Vâ/Tâ). This is why tire pressure increases after riding (friction heats the air inside) and decreases in cold weather. Gay-Lussac's Law shows that pressure and temperature are directly proportional at constant volume (Pâ/Tâ = Pâ/Tâ). The Combined Gas Law unifies these relationships: PâVâ/Tâ = PâVâ/Tâ. All these laws are approximations that work best for ideal gases at moderate temperatures and pressures. The Ideal Gas Law, PV = nRT (where n is moles of gas and R is the gas constant), provides a more complete description. During rapid pumping, the compressed air temperature rises through adiabatic heating, temporarily increasing pressure beyond what would be expected from volume change alone.

scenario.title: Bicycle Pump Laboratory
scenario.content: Students operate a virtual bicycle pump and tire system where they can manipulate pumping speed, ambient temperature, tire volume, and valve operations. The simulation visualizes gas molecules in the pump and tire, showing their movement, collisions, and density changes in real-time. Students can monitor pressure, volume, and temperature gauges while switching between macroscopic views and molecular-level simulations. Interactive graphs plot the relationships between variables, automatically fitting experimental data to theoretical curves. Challenge modes ask students to achieve specific tire pressures under changing conditions or diagnose and solve problems like slow leaks, overheated tires, or pressure changes at different altitudes.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze gas law relationships by examining how pressure, volume, and temperature interact in confined systems. They will predict how changes in one variable affect others under various constraints, and apply gas laws to solve practical problems in everyday contexts.
